extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, peer reviewers, and researchers publishing in Wiley journals
extracted.subtask_description: Organizational best-practice guidelines describing ethical, procedural, and reporting standards for preparing, submitting, reviewing, and publishing scholarly work in Wiley journals, including research integrity, authorship, AI use, data and reporting expectations, and misconduct handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research integrity investigations and escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Research integrity concerns can be raised through the research integrity form; the Integrity Assurance & Case Resolution team will work with the journal’s editor to review and take the appropriate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns will be treated confidentially and assessed in line with COPE guidance; cases needing access to primary data or institutional records will be referred to the relevant research institution, employer, national statutory body, or funder for formal investigation. Input from editorial board members may be sought and amendments made to published articles where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic debate and post-publication critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals encourage academic debate via letters to the editor or correspondence articles; submitting post-publication critique does not guarantee publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters critiquing articles are often peer reviewed and the authors of the original article are usually given an opportunity to respond. When correspondence discusses a published article, Wiley follows COPE guidance on handling post-publication critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals of editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiley journals consider substantiated appeals of editorial decisions if they provide new evidence or information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should submit appeals to the relevant journal using contact details on Wiley Online Library; appeals must provide new evidence or information to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI — review of terms and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should carefully review the terms and conditions, terms of use, and any other conditions or licenses associated with the AI Technology they are considering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must confirm the AI Technology does not claim ownership or copyright of their content or impose limitations that could affect the author’s or Wiley's rights (including the ability to publish). Authors should periodically revisit AI terms to ensure ongoing compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI — human oversight and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may only use AI Technology as an additional tool in their writing process, not a replacement for their own expertise and judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors remain fully responsible for the accuracy of all content and must verify claims, citations, and analyses align with their expertise. They must carefully review AI-generated content to ensure the final work reflects their own expertise, voice, originality, and compliance with Wiley's ethical/editorial standards. The final decision on appropriateness belongs to the journal’s editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI — disclosure of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should document all AI Technology used, including its purpose, influence on key arguments/conclusions, and how they reviewed/verified AI-generated content; they must disclose AI use when submitting a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI tools used solely for spelling, grammar, and general editing are excluded from disclosure requirements. If disclosure is not provided at submission, it may be requested during peer review or after publication. AI must not be used to create, alter, or manipulate original research data or results (including data visualizations, illustrations and photographs).

rubrics_metrics.name: AI — rights protection and licensing concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must not use any AI Technology that restricts their own, Wiley’s, or any other party’s use of the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the AI provider does not gain rights over the author's underlying content, including the right to 'train' their AI Technology on the content; the only acceptable exception is limited access to provide the service. Review terms for clauses on 'ownership', 'data reuse', 'training', or 'opt out'.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI — responsible and ethical use (bias, privacy, neutrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must use AI Technology in a way that aligns with privacy, confidentiality, and compliance obligations and must be aware of potential biases in AI outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using AI to replicate the unique style or voice of others, fact-check AI-generated content for accuracy and neutrality, and remove stereotypes or misinformation. Refer to provided guidance tables for evaluating AI technologies to protect research and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI & Authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: AI Technology is not considered capable of initiating original research and cannot fulfil the role of an author; such tools must not be listed as authors on an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI lacks legal standing and cannot hold or assign copyright; authorship requires accountability for research design and content, which AI cannot provide. See COPE’s position statement on Authorship and AI tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI & Peer review restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors or peer reviewers may use AI Technology to help improve the clarity or quality of written feedback but must disclose that use to the handling editor; editors and peer reviewers are not permitted to upload manuscripts (or any parts) into AI Technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uploading manuscripts to AI may compromise confidentiality, privacy, and copyright; peer review remains a human endeavor and responsibility for accuracy/integrity of peer review rests with the reviewer. Editors may disregard reviewer reports showing signs of inappropriate AI use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship criteria (contribution and accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship gives recognition, accountability, and legal rights; core requirements are a substantial contribution to the research and accountability for the work undertaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorship definitions vary by discipline. Use ORCID iD to distinguish researchers and CRediT contributor roles to describe types of contributions. Contributors who do not qualify for authorship should be acknowledged; minors require guardian consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding author responsibilities and Responsible Corresponding Author (RCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding author ensures all co-authors approve the manuscript and that journal requirements are met, manages communication with the journal, and must be authorized to act for all co-authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple corresponding authors are listed, one RCA must be designated at submission to sign agreements and authorize publication; RCA should remain unchanged throughout the process. Eligibility for APC payments and waivers depends on RCA affiliation at submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship additions, removals, and disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Any authorship additions or removals prior to publication are handled by agreement of the entire author group and must be requested centrally via the editorial office or submission system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All co-authors, including those directly affected, must provide agreement. Reasons will be recorded for transparency. Wiley and journal editors will not adjudicate disputes over whether a contributor qualifies for authorship; COPE recommends agreement on contributors and order prior to submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing editorial-team authorship conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, editorial board members, or journal staff submitting to their own journal should inform the editorial office at submission and include a corresponding statement in the manuscript; they must remove themselves from the decision-making process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Managing Conflicts of Interest: Practical Summary for Editors for further details on recusal and conflict handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author name or pronoun change after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author requests a name or pronoun change after publication, Wiley will update and republish the article discreetly without issuing a correction notice or notifying co-authors to protect privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley will inform indexing services and authors should contact the journal's editorial office to initiate the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceased authors
rubrics_metrics.description: If a manuscript includes a deceased author at submission or an author dies during peer review, Wiley will add an explanatory footnote to the published article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A co-author should confirm the deceased author’s contribution and disclose any conflicts of interest; if the deceased was corresponding author, another co-author must be nominated. Permission from inheritors may be required for transfer agreements not signed prior to death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citations — responsible and non-manipulative citation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing appropriate and relevant literature is a shared responsibility; authors should not engage in excessive self-citation, cite irrelevant sources, or engage in citation manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any type of citation manipulation will result in manuscript rejection. If editors or reviewers request adding citations without a strong scholarly rationale, authors should report this to Wiley's Research integrity team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors, authors, and peer reviewers should disclose interests that might appear to affect objective presentation or review of work, including financial, personal, political, or religious interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include patent ownership, stock ownership, consultancies, or speaker’s fees. Disclosures should be made according to journal policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and intellectual property obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are legally required to sign a copyright agreement before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard author agreements and licensing terms are explained in Wiley's guidance on understanding copyright and licensing; authors must ensure they have the rights to reuse content and that reuse complies with copyright obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections, expressions of concern, retractions, and withdrawals
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiley publishes post-publication notices (retractions, withdrawals, expressions of concern, corrections) to amend the scholarly record as necessary; amendments are not punitive and are permanent and indexable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley works with authors, institutions, and editors to investigate and resolve integrity concerns and uses NISO CREC recommended practices. Authors are encouraged to use the provided Correction template when drafting corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sharing and Data Availability Statement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All research published in Wiley journals must include a Data Availability Statement in accordance with data sharing policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should ensure their statement is accurate and explains how to access or request data. Policies on data sharing are determined by discipline, journal, funder, institution, or legal agreements. Editors may request access to non-public datasets during peer review. Definitions of 'data' include raw/processed data, code, protocols, materials, photographs, and specimens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting guidelines and completeness of methods/results
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must provide sufficient information to allow evaluation, replication, and building upon research; specific journals will list reporting frameworks they require.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discipline-specific frameworks (e.g., EQUATOR Network in health research); journals will detail individual guidelines in author guidelines. Examples include ARRIVE for animal research and SAGER for sex/gender reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell line research reporting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: For cell line research, authors should provide species, sex, tissue of origin, official cell line name, RRID, source/supplier and when obtained, confirmation of authentication (including percentage match and method), and confirmation of mycoplasma-free status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If information is unknown, state this and provide rationale. Further guidance available from ICLAC, NCBI misidentified cell line database, and Cellosaurus problematic cell line database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research based solely on openly available data
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts based solely on openly available data sets must present a clearly defined hypothesis, demonstrate methodological rigor, and include appropriate validation and/or experimental findings to advance knowledge beyond the original data sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mendelian Randomization studies must adhere to specific reporting guidelines and provide a completed checklist on submission. Manuscripts not meeting these criteria may be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) and bias-free language
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiley expects inclusive, respectful practices: authors should use bias-free language and describe study populations accurately; Wiley does not tolerate harassment or discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow APA guidelines for eliminating bias in language. Avoid derogatory demographic descriptors unless essential (e.g., participant quote transparently noted). Describe ethnicity with appropriate terms (e.g., African American, South Asian) rather than race; engage equitable partnerships with local researchers where applicable and respect cultural sensitivities when publishing images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication, falsification, and image manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Data fabrication and falsification are serious breaches: fabrication = inventing findings; falsification = manipulating materials or processes to give a false impression. Inappropriate image manipulation is a form of fabrication/falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some image editing may be legitimate if it does not alter the integrity of underlying data. Authors should retain original unprocessed images and make them available upon request; some journals may require originals alongside processed versions. See Wiley guidelines for preparation of figures for acceptable practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation process for questionable research practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential concerns about questionable research practices (authorship issues, data fabrication, plagiarism, peer review concerns, unethical research) may be raised via the research integrity form and will be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where specific/detailed evidence is provided, an investigation will be conducted by the Integrity Assurance & Case Resolution team. Cases may be referred to institutions for formal investigation and amendments made to published articles as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiley is neutral on any jurisdictional claims; geographical designations and institutional affiliations in published materials reflect the author’s stance and not Wiley’s opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should state their institutional and country/region affiliations. Wiley recognizes a global audience and respects local laws and regulations governing published works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review standards and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is the confidential critical evaluation of a submitted manuscript by subject-matter experts, typically involving at least two independent peer review reports for research manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are selected based on expertise and lack of perceived conflicts of interest. Journals should uphold overarching peer-review standards though specific policies vary; editors adopt the review model best suited to their journal. Peer review is a human endeavor and should not be delegated to AI Technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and text recycling policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism is using another person's ideas, data, or text without proper attribution and is a serious breach; text recycling/self-plagiarism is reusing one's own previous writing without transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley screens manuscripts for duplicated text (e.g., Crossref Similarity Check) and follows COPE guidance on handling plagiarism or text recycling. Some reuse may be acceptable if transparently cited (e.g., methods text), but authors must ensure necessary permissions and cite sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate (redundant) and fragmented publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicate publication is publishing whole or substantial parts of work already published elsewhere without transparency; fragmented ('salami slicing') divides findings into smallest publishable units and is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts must be submitted on the understanding they are not published, in press, or submitted elsewhere. Authors should declare overlapping publications on submission. Wiley follows COPE guidance on handling redundant publication. Some prior dissemination (abstracts, conference posters, preprints, dissertations, datasets) can be acceptable if transparently disclosed and cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable reuse and prior publication exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain prior dissemination/publication can be acceptable and does not constitute duplicate publication if transparently disclosed and cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: abstracts/posters, results presented at meetings, results in databases/registries without interpretation, dissertations/theses in institutional archives, preprints (subject to journal policy), and translations at editor discretion. Transparent co-publication to raise awareness may be considered at editor discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprints policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A preprint is a publicly available manuscript not yet peer reviewed; Wiley encourages submission of manuscripts already available as preprints where permissible by journal policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posting a preprint should not involve assigning copyright; authors should retain copyright and preferably grant 'no re-use' licenses to preprints. Allowing preprints does not guarantee peer review or publication. Use Author Compliance Tool to check individual journal preprint policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human research ethics — approval and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective medical research involving human participants, samples, and data must adhere to recognized ethical standards; authors must confirm ethical approval was received before the study began and include the approver name and approval numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standards like Declaration of Helsinki, Belmont Report, EMA GCP. Authors should provide details on how informed consent was obtained and whether consent for publication was granted. Retrospective ethics approval is generally not accepted; editors may request additional information and may decline manuscripts lacking prospective approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of vulnerable groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must take additional ethical precautions when working with potentially vulnerable groups to ensure truly voluntary participation and appropriate protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider guidance from national bodies and COPE on protecting vulnerable groups. Traditional consent methods may be inappropriate; editors may request more information on consent procedures. Vulnerable groups examples provided (children, refugees, Indigenous peoples, prisoners, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying information and images of participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying information or images of human participants or human remains must not be published unless essential and explicit consent for publication has been obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masking eyes is insufficient. For technical images, remove identifying information including precise geographic origin. Permissions and informed consent for audio/video recordings may be legally required; genetic sequences or family genograms may require consent from multiple family members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research involving organ/tissue donations
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies using donated human organs, tissues or cells must comply with ethics guidance for organ and tissue donation; authors must confirm ethics approval and that procedures complied with relevant international laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should state donor tissue sources and verify donations obtained with informed consent by donor/legal guardian/next of kin. Wiley will not consider manuscripts with data derived from unethically sourced organs or tissue (e.g., executed prisoners). Such manuscripts may be rejected or considered only at editor discretion with prior written request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical trial registration and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiley requires authors to prospectively register clinical trials in a suitable WHO-recommended registry in accordance with WHO policy and the Declaration of Helsinki.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If registered after recruitment began, authors must provide explanation; editors may reject manuscripts if explanation unacceptable. Follow CONSORT guidelines for randomized trials and include registration numbers and registration date in manuscripts. Recommended registries include ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey and retrospective study ethics reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey participants must be informed about the nature/purpose of research and data use/storage; voluntary consent should be obtained and ethical approval where required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For retrospective studies, formal consent requirements vary; authors should consult institutional requirements. If ethical approval is not required or waived, state this in the manuscript. Editors may request additional information and may reject manuscripts lacking sufficient ethical information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal research ethics and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Research involving vertebrates and regulated invertebrates must adhere to international, national, and institutional requirements; authors must confirm ethical approval and provide the approving body's name and approval code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow ARRIVE guidelines and REFLECT for livestock reporting; describe euthanasia and anesthesia methods, endpoints, and steps to reduce suffering (NC3Rs guidance). Images of dead animals should not be shared unless essential. Editors may request additional information and may reject manuscripts not adhering to standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research involving plants and geological samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Research involving plants and geological samples, including collection, must comply with relevant institutional, national, and international guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must confirm fieldwork complied with local legislation and provide evidence of appropriate licenses and permissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual-use research of concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are responsible for identifying whether research could be 'dual-use' — intended for benefit but potentially misapplied to cause harm — and must assess such research for potential risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow WHO and NSABB guidance; dual-use research must undergo institutional review, incorporate risk mitigation, and ensure responsible communication and data dissemination. Editors may reject manuscripts if potential for harm outweighs benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research funding disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must list all funding sources in a dedicated funding section and describe the funder's role beyond providing financial support where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include support for APCs, writing/editorial assistance, or provision of materials. If no specific funding, explicitly state this. Use the Open Funder Registry for guidance on acknowledging funding sources accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher sanctions for questionable practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiley and/or individual journals may impose sanctions (bans on submissions, restrictions on reviewing/editing) on researchers engaging in questionable practices; sanctions are typically time-limited but may be indefinite in severe cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bans are communicated to affected individuals and reviewed upon expiry; sanctions may be appealed by writing to the journal/publisher with new information. Information about sanctions may be shared with individuals responsible for screening across Wiley.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with government sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Wiley must comply with sanctions laws and regulations; editors must take extra care when handling submissions involving sanctioned countries/regions regarding author affiliation, subject matter, and funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should ensure publication is compliant with applicable sanctions laws. Examples of sanctioned countries/regions are listed and may change over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic manipulation of the publication process and paper mills
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic manipulation is when individuals aim to publish research by dishonest or fraudulent means (e.g., subverting peer review, inappropriate authorship practices, citation manipulation, fabricated content); often associated with paper mills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wiley will continue to reject manuscripts or retract articles implicated in systemic manipulation or paper mill activity. Detailed findings of internal investigations may not be shared with all parties to avoid intelligence sharing with bad actors. Wiley participates in initiatives (United2Act, STM Integrity Hub) to address manipulation at scale.
